title: At the Doctor in Spanish: Symptoms, Pain and Appointments
seo_title: At the Doctor in Spanish: Symptoms, Pain and Appointments
meta_description: At the doctor in Spanish: making an appointment, describing symptoms and pain, allergies and medication, understanding instructions, and body vocabulary.
excerpt: Me duele, tengo fiebre, soy alérgico: the phrases you need when you’re unwell.

body_html:
Being at the doctor in Spanish can be stressful, especially when you don’t feel well and need to explain exactly what’s wrong. The good news is that medical conversations follow a clear pattern: you make an appointment, describe your symptoms, answer some questions and receive instructions. This guide gives you the key phrases for each step, plus the body and symptom vocabulary you’re most likely to need. In an emergency, see {{link:emergency-phrases-in-spanish|emergency phrases in Spanish}} and remember that 911 works in the US, Mexico and much of Latin America, while Spain uses 112.

Key takeaways
  • Pain uses doler, like gustar: Me duele la cabeza.
  • Many symptoms use tener: Tengo fiebre, tengo tos.
  • Always mention allergies: Soy alérgico/a a la penicilina.
  • Ask for clarity: ¿Me lo puede repetir más despacio?
{{toc}}

Making an appointment

  • Quería pedir cita con el médico. I’d like to make an appointment with the doctor.
  • ¿Tiene algo para hoy? Do you have anything today?
  • Es urgente. It’s urgent.
  • Tengo seguro médico privado / la tarjeta sanitaria. I have private health insurance / a health card.
  • Tengo cita a las diez. I have an appointment at ten.

Describing symptoms at the doctor in Spanish

SpanishEnglish
Me duele la cabeza / la garganta / el estómago.I have a headache / sore throat / stomach ache.
Tengo fiebre.I have a fever.
Tengo tos.I have a cough.
Estoy mareado/a.I feel dizzy.
Tengo náuseas.I feel nauseous.
He vomitado.I’ve been sick.
Estoy resfriado/a.I have a cold.
No puedo dormir.I can’t sleep.

Doler works like gustar: the painful body part is the subject, so plural parts need duelen: Me duelen los pies. See {{link:how-to-use-gustar|how to use gustar}}. Also note the article with body parts: la cabeza, not mi cabeza.

Describing pain

  • Me duele aquí. It hurts here.
  • Es un dolor fuerte / leve / constante. It’s a strong / mild / constant pain.
  • Me duele cuando respiro. It hurts when I breathe.
  • Empezó hace tres días. It started three days ago.
  • Va y viene. It comes and goes.
{{image:2}}

Questions the doctor may ask

  • ¿Qué le pasa? What’s the matter?
  • ¿Desde cuándo? Since when?
  • ¿Toma algún medicamento? Are you taking any medication?
  • ¿Es alérgico/a a algo? Are you allergic to anything?
  • ¿Le duele si aprieto aquí? Does it hurt if I press here?
  • Respire hondo. Breathe deeply.

Doctors usually use usted; see {{link:tu-vs-usted|tú vs usted}}.

Medical history, allergies and medication

  • Soy alérgico/a a la penicilina. I’m allergic to penicillin.
  • Tengo diabetes / asma. I have diabetes / asthma.
  • Estoy embarazada. I’m pregnant. (and only if you are; see {{link:embarrassing-spanish-mistakes|embarrassing Spanish mistakes}})
  • Tomo pastillas para la tensión. I take tablets for blood pressure.
{{book:the-mind-lies}}

Understanding instructions

  • Le voy a recetar un antibiótico. I’m going to prescribe an antibiotic.
  • Tómese una pastilla cada ocho horas. Take one tablet every eight hours.
  • En ayunas / con las comidas. On an empty stomach / with meals.
  • Haga reposo. Rest.
  • Vuelva si no mejora. Come back if it doesn’t improve.
  • Aquí tiene la receta. Here’s the prescription.

If anything is unclear, ask: ¿Me lo puede escribir? (Can you write it down for me?) or ¿Cuántas veces al día? (How many times a day?). Never guess about medication. The RAE dictionary lists receta as both a prescription and a recipe, so context matters.

A sample consultation

  • Doctor: Buenos días. ¿Qué le pasa?
  • You: Me duele mucho la garganta y tengo fiebre desde ayer. (My throat really hurts and I’ve had a fever since yesterday.)
  • Doctor: ¿Es alérgico a algún medicamento?
  • You: No, que yo sepa. (Not that I know of.)
  • Doctor: Tiene amigdalitis. Le receto un antibiótico. Una pastilla cada doce horas durante siete días.

Practical tips

Before your appointment, write down your symptoms, when they started and any medication you take, in Spanish if you can. Bring your passport or health card, and your insurance details if you’re traveling. In Spain, you go first to your médico de cabecera (Primary care doctor) at the centro de salud; for emergencies, it’s urgencias at a hospital. Pharmacists are also very helpful for minor problems; see {{link:get-well-soon-in-spanish|get well soon in Spanish}} for what friends will say afterward.

Body vocabulary

A few body parts you are likely to need: la cabeza (head), la garganta (throat), el pecho (chest), el estómago or la tripa (stomach, tummy), la espalda (back), el oído (inner ear) and la oreja (outer ear), la muela (back tooth), la rodilla (knee), el tobillo (ankle). Notice that an earache is dolor de oído, not de oreja, and a toothache is usually dolor de muelas. With these words and me duele, you can describe most everyday problems clearly. If you are traveling, it also helps to know el seguro de viaje (travel insurance) and el informe médico (medical report), which you may need for a claim.

Common mistakes

MistakeBetterWhy
Mi cabeza duele.Me duele la cabeza.Doler + article
Me duele los pies.Me duelen los pies.Plural subject
Estoy constipado (constipated)Estoy estreñido.Constipado = a cold
Soy fiebre.Tengo fiebre.Symptoms with tener
{{image:3}}

Final thoughts

Use me duele for pain, tengo for symptoms, mention allergies and medication, and ask the doctor to repeat or write things down. Prepare a few notes beforehand and you’ll communicate clearly when it matters. For more everyday situations, see {{link:spanish-phrases-for-everyday-situations|my guide to Spanish phrases for everyday situations}}.

faq.q: How do you say “it hurts” in Spanish?
faq.a: Me duele (one thing) or Me duelen (several), with the body part and an article: Me duele la cabeza, Me duelen los pies.

faq.q: How do you make a doctor’s appointment in Spanish?
faq.a: Quería pedir cita con el médico. You can add ¿Tiene algo para hoy? or Es urgente.

faq.q: How do you say you’re allergic to something in Spanish?
faq.a: Soy alérgico (male) or alérgica (female) a…: Soy alérgica a la penicilina.
